hotels.whyGo: The same lived-in lobby format as the Shoreditch original, minutes from the British Museum rather than the bar strip - the calmer of the two.
hotels.opNote: Breakfast bag included, same as the other Hoxtons. Recently refreshed rooms across the estate - ask whether a specific room has had the update if it matters.

hotels.name: The Hoxton, Shoreditch
hotels.style: The original of the format
hotels.whyGo: The hotel that made the open-lobby-as-workspace format normal, and still the best example of it - the ground floor is genuinely full of locals, not just guests.
hotels.opNote: Breakfast is a bag hung on your door, included in the rate. Room grades are named by SIZE - a Shoebox is exactly what it says.

hotels.name: The Hoxton, Southwark
hotels.style: Post-industrial salvage aesthetic
hotels.whyGo: The Hoxton format applied to a Southwark new-build, with Seabird - a rooftop restaurant with the longest oyster list in London - on top.
hotels.opNote: Breakfast bag included in the rate, as at every Hoxton. Seabird on the roof is open to non-residents and needs booking.

hotels.name: The Kensington Hotel
hotels.style: Regency townhouses, museum quarter
hotels.whyGo: A row of Regency townhouses on Queen's Gate, a few minutes from the Natural History Museum and the V&A - the museum quarter without being on the Cromwell Road.
hotels.opNote: Three of the four South Kensington sources, the strongest in that corpus. Doyle Collection, same group as The Marylebone and The Bloomsbury.

hotels.name: The LaLiT London
hotels.style: Indian-owned hotel in a listed former grammar school
hotels.whyGo: Seventy rooms in the Grade II listed former St Olave's Grammar School, designed in the 1890s by E.W. Mountford, architect of the Old Bailey. The rooms are called classrooms, some run to thirty-foot ceilings, and Baluchi serves Indian food in the old assembly hall under blue chandeliers.
hotels.opNote: THE HOTEL'S OWN COPY PLACES IT 'IN THE HEART OF THE CITY OF LONDON'. It is not: it is on Tooley Street on the south bank, six minutes' walk from London Bridge station by the operator's own reckoning, and the guides that named it put it in Bermondsey. The room names are a school joke rather than a size guide, so the entry room is a 'Cosy Classroom' and the top one a LaLiT Legacy Suite. Opened 2017 in a building that was a school from 1561 to 1967. Named by 2 independent domains.

hotels.name: The Laslett
hotels.style: Named for local artists and writers
hotels.whyGo: Every room named after a local artist, writer or musician associated with Notting Hill, on the doorstep of Portobello Road.
hotels.opNote: Right on Notting Hill Gate, so it is the most convenient of the area's boutiques for the Central and Circle lines.

hotels.name: The Lost Poet
hotels.style: Four rooms in a Victorian Portobello Road townhouse
hotels.whyGo: Four individually decorated rooms in a Victorian townhouse at the very top of Portobello Road, done out with bold wallpapers, modern art and reclaimed panelling from old school science labs - the antiques market starts at the door.
hotels.opNote: IT IS A GUEST HOUSE, NOT AN APARTMENT LET - it sells four rooms nightly through its own booking engine, with a 3pm check-in and an 11am check-out. There is no 24-hour desk: check-in is online with keyless entry, staff are on site 8am to 6pm and it is phone support outside those hours. Two domains in the Notting Hill corpus.

hotels.name: The Megaro
hotels.style: Mural-fronted hotel opposite King's Cross
hotels.whyGo: A 40-room independent recognisable from the street by the giant graffiti-style mural covering its whole facade, individually designed rooms and about as close to St Pancras as a hotel gets outside the Renaissance itself.
hotels.opNote: Genuinely independent and personally run, which shows in the service compared with the chains nearby. Small enough to book out for a Eurostar-timed stay.

hotels.name: The Mitre, Hampton Court
hotels.style: Riverside boutique hotel facing Hampton Court Palace
hotels.whyGo: On the bank of the Thames directly opposite Hampton Court Palace, with rooms named after Henry VIII, his wives and his hobbies, a riverside terrace, the 1665 Brasserie and an orangery that does afternoon tea.
hotels.opNote: NOT IN LONDON: East Molesey, Surrey, outside every neighbourhood on this sheet - which is the point of it, and the reason the guides reach for it. Hampton Court station is a three-minute walk and runs into Waterloo. Parking is on site but first-come and £7 a night, dogs are welcome in selected rooms, accessible rooms exist but need to be arranged by phone, and there is no spa. Two domains in the general hotels corpus. DO NOT CONFUSE with The Mitre at 6 Holland Park Avenue, W11 - a different pub with rooms, and the one All Around London names in the Notting Hill corpus.

hotels.name: The Montague on the Gardens
hotels.style: Georgian townhouse with a garden terrace, beside the British Museum
hotels.whyGo: Next door to the British Museum, with a raised garden terrace over a private square - Bloomsbury's one hotel that makes something of the garden squares rather than just sitting among them.
hotels.opNote: Three domains in the Bloomsbury corpus, the only property to reach three there, and named again in the dog-friendly pass. Red Carnation, so the same group as The Rubens and The Milestone, both already ours.

hotels.name: The Newman
hotels.style: Fitzrovia boutique, restaurant-led
hotels.whyGo: A small Fitzrovia hotel in the block behind Oxford Street, close enough to Soho and Marylebone to use both without staying in either.
hotels.opNote: Three guides in the general pass and three again in the boutique pass, which is unusually consistent for a new opening. NEEDS VERIFYING - the operator's site did not respond, so the street address and star rating are unconfirmed.

hotels.name: The Pelican
hotels.style: Rooms over a well-regarded gastropub
hotels.whyGo: Rooms above one of the better gastropubs in west London, on All Saints Road a few minutes off Portobello.
hotels.opNote: A small pub with rooms rather than a hotel - no lift, no reception desk in the hotel sense. The dining room is the draw and books ahead.

hotels.name: The Petersham Hotel
hotels.style: Victorian hotel above the river meadows
hotels.whyGo: Perched above Petersham Meadows with the same protected river view Turner painted, a short walk from the top of Richmond Hill.
hotels.opNote: Book a river-view room specifically - standard rooms do not face the Thames. Steep walk down to the towpath and back up.

hotels.name: The Portobello Hotel
hotels.style: Eccentric Victorian townhouse
hotels.roomTypes: Double, suite, some with round beds and freestanding baths
hotels.whyGo: A 21-room Victorian townhouse on a quiet garden square, favoured by musicians and actors since the 1970s for exactly the reason it still works - nobody bothers you.
hotels.opNote: A townhouse with no lift, so upper rooms mean stairs with luggage. Some of the more theatrical rooms - round beds, claw-foot baths in the room itself - are not for everyone; ask before booking.

hotels.name: The Princess Royal
hotels.style: Four bedrooms over a Cubitt House Notting Hill pub
hotels.whyGo: Four bedrooms named after princesses above a Cubitt House pub, with a light-flooded conservatory, two terraces planted by the garden designer Jinny Blom and a seasonal British and modern European kitchen downstairs.
hotels.opNote: A PUB WITH ROOMS, NOT A HOTEL - four bedrooms only, over a working pub that also runs two private feasting rooms, so book early and expect noise from below at weekends. The address is W2, on the Bayswater side of Notting Hill a few minutes from Westbourne Grove, although the operator and both guides call it Notting Hill. Two domains in the Notting Hill corpus.

hotels.name: The Rosebery by Supercity Aparthotels
hotels.style: Apartments on Rosebery Avenue
hotels.whyGo: On the Clerkenwell edge of Islington, ten minutes from Farringdon and its Elizabeth line platforms, with Exmouth Market's restaurants at the end of the road.
hotels.opNote: One of the better-placed aparthotels for eating out, which is the usual weakness of the format. NOT PRICED YET - no rate has been sampled for this row.

hotels.name: The Rubens at the Palace
hotels.style: Traditional, opposite the Royal Mews
hotels.whyGo: Directly opposite the Royal Mews, a two-minute walk from Buckingham Palace and under two blocks from Victoria station.
hotels.opNote: The closest genuinely comfortable hotel to Buckingham Palace and the Royal Mews on foot. Traditional, family-run styling rather than a design hotel.

hotels.name: The Standard, London
hotels.style: Brutalist 1970s town hall annexe
hotels.whyGo: A preserved 1974 Brutalist town hall annexe directly opposite St Pancras, with Shawn Hausman interiors described as Stanley Kubrick through the colour lens of Wes Anderson.
hotels.opNote: Decimo, the tenth-floor tapas restaurant, has the view. The external red lift running up the outside of the building is worth requesting a room near.

hotels.name: The Trafalgar St. James
hotels.style: Curio Collection hotel on the corner of Trafalgar Square
hotels.whyGo: On the corner of Trafalgar Square itself, with a rooftop bar over the square, Rockwell Bistro and Wine Bar at street level, and new Spring Garden Suites in a quiet corner of the building - some with access to a subterranean garden.
hotels.opNote: Both guides that named it, named it for THE ROOFTOP, which takes non-residents as well as guests, so it is busy on summer evenings. Part of Hilton's Curio Collection, so Hilton Honors applies. Also picked up by a wheelchair-travel guide in the accessible corpus; that has not been checked against the operator, so no accessibility claim is made here.

hotels.name: The Zetter Bloomsbury
hotels.style: Georgian townhouse row steps from the British Museum
hotels.whyGo: The Zetter's newest house, opened in April 2026 across a run of Georgian townhouses on Montague Street beside the British Museum, with a garden, a gym and the Parlour and Orangery for long cocktail afternoons.
hotels.opNote: NOT THE ZETTER TOWNHOUSE MARYLEBONE, which this sheet already holds - a separate and much newer property; the group now runs three houses, Clerkenwell, Marylebone and Bloomsbury. Opened April 2026, so it is thinly reviewed and the operator's own page still carries an "Opening April 2026" line. Three domains in the general corpus, the strongest evidence in this batch.

hotels.name: The Zetter Townhouse Marylebone
hotels.style: Eccentric British townhouse
hotels.whyGo: A Georgian townhouse decorated like an eccentric relative's home - taxidermy, clashing prints, and a cocktail lounge that is a destination in its own right.
hotels.opNote: Small and stair-heavy in places despite the lift. The ground-floor bar gets busy with non-residents, which is either the charm or the problem.

hotels.name: Town Hall Hotel
hotels.style: Edwardian town hall turned hotel
hotels.whyGo: A 1910 town hall with the council chamber and marble staircases intact, a 14-metre heated pool, and the two-Michelin-starred Da Terra in the building.
hotels.opNote: TIME OUT'S BEST HOTEL IN LONDON. In Bethnal Green rather than the centre, which is the trade and the reason it costs half what a comparable central room would.

hotels.name: Treehouse Hotel London
hotels.style: Playful, sustainable, top-floor views
hotels.whyGo: Occupies the top floors next to BBC Broadcasting House, so every room has a panorama - and the rooms come with magic 8 balls, cuckoo clocks and Paddington Bears without tipping into gimmick.
hotels.opNote: Time Out gave it FIVE out of five, calling it everything you could want from a sustainable yet high-end hotel in London's busiest district. The rooftop bar is open to non-residents.

hotels.name: Virgin Hotels London-Shoreditch
hotels.style: Design hotel with a year-round rooftop pool
hotels.whyGo: A heated rooftop pool and terrace open all year over Shoreditch, which is the reason guests pick this over the area's other design hotels. Virgin Hotels' first London property, and the third name on this building - it was The Curtain, then Mondrian Shoreditch, and has been Virgin since August 2024.
hotels.opNote: The rooftop pool and bar draw a non-resident crowd at weekends - book a pool slot rather than assuming it will be quiet.

hotels.name: Wilde Aparthotels Covent Garden
hotels.style: Studios with kitchens, central
hotels.whyGo: A kitchen and a washing machine in the middle of the West End, which removes the single biggest cost of a London family trip - eating out three times a day.
hotels.opNote: Studios rather than separate bedrooms, so a family shares one room. Check the floor plan before booking for four. SOLD TWICE ON HOTELS.COM, as Wilde Covent Garden and as Wilde by Staycity The Strand - the same building at 11 Adam Street under two listings, so compare both before booking. NOTE: the only named press review found for this brand covers Wilde's Paddington site, not this one - the two are different buildings and should not be assumed identical.

hotels.name: 1 Hotel Mayfair
hotels.style: Eco-luxury, reclaimed timber and planting throughout
hotels.whyGo: The sustainability-first hotel brand's first London house, on Berkeley Street - reclaimed materials, heavy planting, and a green agenda carried far enough that it shapes the rooms rather than just the marketing.
hotels.opNote: Named by five independent guides in the general pass, more than anything else in it. No first-hand community account found yet.

hotels.name: 45 Park Lane
hotels.style: Forty-five rooms, every one facing Hyde Park
hotels.whyGo: Forty-five rooms and suites and, on the operator's own account, every one of them overlooks Hyde Park, with the higher floors taking in the rest of London. Wolfgang Puck's CUT is the house steak restaurant and Sushi Kanesaka holds its Michelin star behind a separate door.
hotels.opNote: The best-evidenced property in this batch - six independent domains across six corpora, including the luxury, Mayfair, family, spa and views passes as well as the general one. The Dorchester Collection's small London house rather than its grand one, and it sits across Park Lane from The Dorchester itself. The site offers guest access to a subterranean spa and Park Lane's longest pool without saying which building holds it, so confirm at booking.

hotels.name: art'otel London Battersea Power Station
hotels.style: Design hotel with a rooftop pool
hotels.whyGo: Jaime Hayon's bold, colourful design throughout, a rooftop pool over the Power Station chimneys, and named Hotel of the Year 2025 by The Caterer.
hotels.opNote: Inside the Battersea Power Station development itself, so the shops, bars and Lift 109 are all a lift ride away rather than a walk.

hotels.name: art'otel London Hoxton
hotels.style: D*Face-designed tower with a 25th-floor restaurant
hotels.whyGo: A 26-storey tower wrapped in twisted black fins, with the street artist D*Face's work running through every room and public space. There is a public gallery, a 60-seat screening room, and an indoor pool non-residents can book. Two original Banksys, rescued from The Foundry which stood on this site, are preserved on the outside of the building and free to see from the street.
hotels.opNote: NEEDS VERIFYING - marketed as "a five-star experience" but no official star classification found, so starRating is deliberately blank. Sources conflict on 26 vs 27 storeys. Solaya, the 25th-floor restaurant, is closed Sundays and Mondays. Breakfast is about £56 extra. Pool day access for non-residents was £65 (11:00-16:00) when checked.

hotels.name: At Sloane
hotels.style: Costes-run five-star private house by Sloane Square
hotels.whyGo: Thirty bedrooms off Sloane Square done by the French architect-decorator Francois-Joseph Graf for the Costes group, so it reads as a Parisian private house rather than a London hotel. The dining room is on the sixth floor and serves 24/7, and there is a 'secret bar' open late.
hotels.opNote: Four named sources and all four are Conde Nast titles - Traveller UK, Traveler US, Vogue UK, House and Garden - so this is one publisher's taste rather than four independent opinions. The operator styles the name with a leading ellipsis, '...At Sloane', which is why it sorts oddly in guide lists and why the candidate file recorded it that way.

hotels.name: Beaverbrook Town House
hotels.style: Fourteen suites named after London theatres
hotels.whyGo: Two restored Georgian houses on Sloane Street run as one hotel of fourteen suites, each named for a London theatre and hung with vintage posters, looking out over Cadogan Gardens. The Fuji Grill does Japanese downstairs and Sir Frank's is the bar.
hotels.opNote: SUITES ONLY - fourteen of them and no standard rooms, so there is no cheaper tier to drop to. The country sister is Beaverbrook in Leatherhead and the group sells a two-centre 'Town to Country' stay between them. Three domains named it and all three are Conde Nast titles, so treat the count as one publisher.

hotels.name: Broadwick Soho
hotels.style: Maximalist independent, 57 rooms
hotels.whyGo: Leopard print, velvet and clashing colour by Martin Brudnizki, built by a group of friends rather than a hotel group - and named the UK's best hotel at the 2026 Muddy Stilettos Awards, beating out the country's grandest countryside piles.
hotels.opNote: NATIONAL AWARD, not a London-only one - it beat entries from Bath, Hampshire, Wiltshire and Kent to take the UK title. Fifty-seven rooms, so it is small and books out.

hotels.name: Brown's Hotel
hotels.style: London's first hotel, since 1837
hotels.whyGo: Opened 1837 and generally called London's first hotel - Kipling wrote here, Bell made the first British telephone call from it, and Agatha Christie set At Bertram's Hotel on it.
hotels.opNote: A Michelin Key. The Drawing Room afternoon tea is open to non-residents and is the traditional way in.

hotels.name: Charlotte Street Hotel
hotels.style: Firmdale boho-chic on the restaurant street
hotels.whyGo: Fifty-two boho-chic rooms with a private screening room and a walk-in position on Charlotte Street itself, the densest restaurant run in central London.
hotels.opNote: The screening room can be booked privately, which is an unusual amenity to have on the doorstep of a dinner reservation rather than across town.

hotels.name: Cheval Phoenix House
hotels.style: Apartments a street from Sloane Square
hotels.whyGo: One street back from Sloane Square, which puts the King's Road, Belgravia and the Royal Court all within a few minutes' walk.
hotels.opNote: A residential street rather than a hotel strip, and priced as Chelsea. Full kitchens and a concierge. NOT PRICED YET - no rate has been sampled for this row.

hotels.name: Cheval Three Quays
hotels.style: River-facing apartments beside the Tower
hotels.whyGo: Directly on the river between the Tower of London and Tower Bridge, with apartments that look straight at both - the view is what you are paying for and it is the best of any aparthotel in London.
hotels.opNote: Full kitchens, a concierge and one- to three-bedroom layouts, so it works for a family in a way a hotel room at this price does not. NOT PRICED YET - no rate has been sampled for this row.

hotels.name: Claridge's
hotels.style: Art deco Mayfair institution
hotels.whyGo: The art deco hotel other London hotels are measured against, and the only London property on Conde Nast Traveller's 2026 Gold List.
hotels.opNote: Afternoon tea books months ahead and is the affordable way to see the building without a room. Dress code is enforced in the public rooms.

hotels.name: COMO The Halkin
hotels.style: Belgravia townhouse, Armani-uniformed, Thai kitchen
hotels.whyGo: COMO's first hotel, on a Belgravia side street, with Ametsa - a Basque kitchen with a Michelin star - on the ground floor and only forty-one rooms above it.
hotels.opNote: Three domains once the two spellings are treated as one hotel: sources write it as both "The Halkin" and "COMO The Halkin", which the extractor scored as two separate properties at two domains each. Same building, verified.

hotels.name: Corinthia London
hotels.style: Whitehall grand, with a four-floor spa
hotels.whyGo: Two Michelin Keys, a Baccarat chandelier of a thousand crystals in the lobby, and a spa running across four floors - the largest of any London hotel.
hotels.opNote: Between Trafalgar Square and the river, so Westminster and the South Bank are both walkable. Seven penthouse suites sit at the top.

hotels.name: Covent Garden Hotel
hotels.style: Firmdale, Kit Kemp interiors, Monmouth Street
hotels.whyGo: Kit Kemp's Firmdale house on Monmouth Street in Seven Dials, with the drawing room and the private screening room that the group is known for.
hotels.opNote: Three of the Covent Garden sources and two in the general pass. Seven Dials rather than the piazza, which is the quieter half.

hotels.name: Dorset Square Hotel
hotels.style: Firmdale's first hotel, cricket in every room
hotels.whyGo: Tim and Kit Kemp's very first hotel, in a Regency building looking onto the garden square that was Thomas Lord's original cricket ground - the 38 bedrooms carry cricket artwork and memorabilia because of it, and The Potting Shed downstairs names its cocktails after the same history.
hotels.opNote: The smallest and quietest of Firmdale's London houses and the one in a residential street rather than a shopping one; the operator puts Marylebone station five minutes' walk away and Baker Street ten. Star rating is not stated on the operator's own page, so it is left blank here rather than assumed from the group's other hotels. Two clean domains: Time Out in the Marylebone pass and Conde Nast Traveller in the family pass.

hotels.name: Four Seasons Hotel London at Park Lane
hotels.style: Eleven storeys above Hyde Park Corner, spa on the roof
hotels.whyGo: The rooftop spa is the thing - a glass box on the tenth floor looking over Hyde Park, which almost no London hotel can offer because almost none has the height in Mayfair.
hotels.opNote: The most-named property of the whole second pass: four domains in the Mayfair corpus and a mention in five others. Not to be confused with Four Seasons at Tower Bridge, which is a separate hotel and only reached two.

hotels.name: Four Seasons Hotel London at Tower Bridge
hotels.style: The old Port of London Authority headquarters
hotels.whyGo: The former Port of London Authority headquarters at Ten Trinity Square, a listed 1920s pile beside Tower Hill, converted into a Four Seasons - the Grand Heritage Suites run to ceilings of five metres and the third-floor Royal Garden Suite opens onto its own planted terrace.
hotels.opNote: RENAMED IN OCTOBER 2024. This was Four Seasons Hotel London at Ten Trinity Square and plenty of live guides still call it that, so watch for it arriving twice under two names. The same building holds the Ten Trinity Square private members' club - a Reignwood, Chateau Latour and Four Seasons venture - which is separate from the hotel and members-only, so a guest is not automatically inside it. Two domains, both luxury-travel titles.

hotels.name: Fulham Pier Hotel
hotels.style: Thirteen river-facing rooms in the Fulham Pier building
hotels.whyGo: Thirteen rooms with floor-to-ceiling windows onto the Thames, inside the seven-floor Fulham Pier building on Stevenage Road - booking a room gets you into Lighthouse Social, the members' club in the same building, plus a food hall of more than ten vendors and two rooftop bars.
hotels.opNote: THE SPA AND THE ROOFTOP INFINITY POOL ARE NOT OPEN YET. The operator's own FAQ calls the spa 'anticipated to open in summer' with no confirmed date, lists the wellness floors and the pool as 'opening winter', and says there is no hotel gym at all - it points guests to gyms nearby. NO TUBE ON THE DOORSTEP: Putney Bridge is 0.7 miles, which the operator itself calls a 10 to 20 minute walk through Bishops Park. And Fulham Pier's own site says the destination closes for a limited number of Fulham FC match days each year, with a match-day traffic order on the surrounding streets - so check your dates against the match-day list before booking for the food hall and the club. Both sources are Conde Nast, UK and US editions of one magazine, which makes this the thinnest evidence in the batch.

hotels.name: Ham Yard Hotel
hotels.style: Firmdale's Soho flagship round a garden
hotels.whyGo: Two Michelin Keys, built from the ground up around a tree-filled courtyard with a Tony Cragg bronze, and a 1950s bowling alley in the basement.
hotels.opNote: Kit Kemp's patterns throughout, as at Charlotte Street. The bowling alley and the roof terrace are bookable without a room.

hotels.name: Hotel Café Royal
hotels.style: Regency grandeur on Regent Street
hotels.whyGo: Two Michelin Keys, a grand nineteenth-century building on the Soho edge of Regent Street, and the Akasha spa that Time Out named London's best in 2025.
hotels.opNote: The Grill Room and the Oscar Wilde Lounge are open to non-residents and are the affordable way to see the interiors.

hotels.name: InterContinental London - The O2
hotels.style: Modern tower on the Peninsula
hotels.whyGo: A glass tower on the river with a spa and pool looking straight across to Canary Wharf, attached to The O2 for anyone catching a show there.
hotels.opNote: On the Peninsula rather than in Greenwich town - a DLR or riverboat ride from the Cutty Sark and the Observatory, not a walk.

hotels.name: Jumeirah Carlton Tower
hotels.style: Cadogan Place tower with a panoramic health club
hotels.whyGo: Guests get a private key to the Cadogan Place gardens, which are locked to everyone else on the square, and The Peak health club at the top of the building has a naturally lit indoor pool and a view over the skyline - two things a Knightsbridge hotel of this size almost never has together.
hotels.opNote: RENAMED. The two Belgravia sources that named it write 'The Carlton Tower Jumeirah'; the operator now trades as JUMEIRAH CARLTON TOWER and the old URL redirects to the new one. Two domains in the Belgravia corpus plus one in the family pass. 186 rooms. HOOD IS A JUDGEMENT CALL: Jumeirah's own contact block says 'On Cadogan Place, Knightsbridge', the corpus that surfaced it is the Belgravia one, and the nearest row on this sheet - The Cadogan at 75 Sloane Street - is filed Chelsea. Knightsbridge here because that is the operator's word; borough follows The Cadogan.

hotels.name: Mandarin Oriental Hyde Park
hotels.style: The group's original London house, backing onto Hyde Park
hotels.whyGo: The back of the hotel opens straight into Hyde Park and the front onto Knightsbridge, so Harrods and Sloane Street are on one side and the Diana Memorial Playground is a walk across the park on the other. Dinner by Heston Blumenthal and The Aubrey, a Japanese izakaya, are both in the building.
hotels.opNote: MANDARIN ORIENTAL NOW HAS TWO LONDON HOTELS and this sheet already carries the other one - Mandarin Oriental Mayfair, at 22 Hanover Square. This is the Knightsbridge original, and the two are easy to book by mistake; the group's own navigation lists them as 'London - Hyde Park' and 'London - Mayfair'. Parking is valet only and charged, and the hotel asks you to arrange it with the concierge in advance because of the traffic on Knightsbridge. A Connecting & Family Rooms category is sold, which is why the family lists name it. Named by 2 independent domains.

hotels.name: Mandarin Oriental Mayfair
hotels.style: The group's second London house
hotels.whyGo: Only fifty rooms, which makes it the most intimate of the recent Mayfair openings, on Hanover Square a minute from Oxford Circus.
hotels.opNote: Small by design and sold out far ahead. The group's original Hyde Park property is a different hotel entirely - check which one you are booking.

hotels.name: Native Mayfair
hotels.style: Apartments on a Mayfair mews
hotels.whyGo: On a mews off Grosvenor Square, three minutes from Bond Street and its Elizabeth line platforms - a kitchen in the middle of Mayfair, which is close to unheard of.
hotels.opNote: The most expensive of the Native addresses and the one where the apartment format saves the most, because eating out nearby is Mayfair money. NOT PRICED YET - no rate has been sampled for this row.

hotels.name: No.5 Maddox Street
hotels.style: All-apartment Mayfair address, one to three bedrooms
hotels.whyGo: Every unit is a whole apartment with a kitchen - the smallest 27 sq m, the largest a three-bed of 79 sq m with outdoor space - on a quiet side street a minute off Regent Street, which is a rare thing to book in Mayfair for either two nights or two months.
hotels.opNote: NOT A HOTEL PRODUCT ANY MORE, whatever the guides that name it imply: the operator sells serviced apartments with a concierge team, housekeeping and preferential rates at a nearby gym, not rooms with a front desk and a restaurant. Some apartments have private terraces and some do not, and the operator marks that with an asterisk rather than by room type. Run by Living Rooms, the same operator as The Laslett in Notting Hill, which is already on this sheet. Two guide domains.

hotels.name: Nobu Hotel London Portman Square
hotels.style: Nobu's Marylebone house, restaurant-led, on a garden square
hotels.whyGo: The quieter of Nobu's two London hotels - a garden square in Marylebone rather than Shoreditch - with the Nobu restaurant, its terrace, the bar and afternoon tea all downstairs, and Marylebone High Street, Mayfair and Oxford Street each a walk away.
hotels.opNote: TWO NOBU HOTELS IN LONDON and the guides use short forms that do not separate them - this is Portman Square in Marylebone, not Nobu Hotel London Shoreditch, which appears in our dog-friendly corpus under a name a reader would confuse with this one. The operator itself shortens the name to "Nobu Portman Square" on its own site, so both spellings are legitimate. Three guide domains.

hotels.name: NoMad London
hotels.style: Theatrical, in the old Bow Street Magistrates' Court
hotels.whyGo: The former Bow Street Magistrates' Court, opposite the Royal Opera House - the building where the Bow Street Runners were founded and where Oscar Wilde was remanded, now a hotel that leans into all of it.
hotels.opNote: Five guides in the general pass plus three in the Covent Garden pass. Runs under Hilton's LXR collection, so Hilton Honors applies.

hotels.name: One Aldwych
hotels.style: Edwardian bank building, chlorine-free pool
hotels.whyGo: The old Morning Post building on the Aldwych corner, with a swimming pool that plays underwater music and no chlorine in it - the theatres are a five-minute walk in either direction.
hotels.opNote: Three of the Covent Garden sources and two in the family pass. Genuinely central for theatre, which is what most people staying here want.

hotels.name: Raffles London at The OWO
hotels.style: The Old War Office, reborn
hotels.whyGo: The Old War Office on Whitehall, where Churchill planned D-Day and Ian Fleming worked in naval intelligence, converted into 120 rooms with butler service.
hotels.opNote: Nine restaurants and bars on site, several open to non-residents - the cheapest way into the building without a room. Directly on Whitehall, so Downing Street and the Churchill War Rooms are a walk.

hotels.name: Rosewood London
hotels.style: Edwardian Belle Époque courtyard
hotels.whyGo: Two Michelin Keys, entered through a carriageway into a Belle Époque courtyard that cuts the noise of High Holborn out completely.
hotels.opNote: Between Covent Garden and Bloomsbury, walkable to both. Scarfes Bar has live jazz nightly and is open to non-residents.

hotels.name: Shangri-La The Shard, London
hotels.style: The highest hotel in western Europe
hotels.whyGo: Floors 34 to 52 of the Shard, with the infinity pool on the 52nd floor giving a view over London that no other hotel in the city can offer at any price.
hotels.opNote: One of the highest-scoring hotels found in this pass - 9.1 across nearly 3,000 reviews. The view is genuinely the product; a lower floor room here defeats the point.

hotels.name: Six Senses London
hotels.style: Wellness hotel in the old Whiteleys
hotels.whyGo: Six Senses' first UK property, inside the Grade II Whiteleys department store, with a spa running a magnesium pool and cryotherapy.
hotels.opNote: Opened after a three-year delay. The spa is the reason to choose it over the Mayfair five-stars, and it is bookable by non-residents.

hotels.name: St Pancras Renaissance Hotel London
hotels.style: Gothic Revival railway hotel
hotels.whyGo: George Gilbert Scott's 1873 Gothic Revival masterpiece, restored after decades of dereliction, attached directly to the Eurostar terminal at St Pancras.
hotels.opNote: The building the Spice Girls filmed 'Wannabe' on the staircase of - a fact almost every guide mentions and almost every guest asks about. Book the Chambers Suites for the original 1873 rooms.

hotels.name: The Beaumont Mayfair
hotels.style: Art deco, with a sculpture you sleep inside
hotels.roomTypes: Double, suite, ROOM by Antony Gormley
hotels.whyGo: Two Michelin Keys, an art deco building on Brown Hart Gardens - and ROOM, an Antony Gormley sculpture bolted to the facade that you can book and sleep inside.
hotels.opNote: ROOM is a genuine Gormley artwork containing a bedroom, priced far above the standard rooms and booked months out. The rest of the hotel is a straightforwardly excellent deco five-star.

hotels.name: The Berkeley
hotels.style: Knightsbridge grande dame with a rooftop pool
hotels.whyGo: The third Maybourne house after Claridge's and The Connaught, and the one with the rooftop pool - it opens to the sky in summer, which almost nothing else in central London does.
hotels.opNote: The strongest evidence of anything in this batch: five guides in the general pass, five again in the family pass, and a first-hand recommendation on r/FATTravel - "just got back... the location was ideal".

hotels.name: The Cadogan, A Belmond Hotel
hotels.style: Storied Sloane Street institution
hotels.whyGo: A Sloane Street address with a genuine history of hosting dignitaries and celebrities, restored by Belmond and consistently one of the best-reviewed hotels in the city.
hotels.opNote: One of the highest guest-rating scores of any hotel in London - 97% in the surveys collected. On Sloane Street itself, so the King's Road shops are a short walk.

hotels.name: The Chancery Rosewood
hotels.style: All-suite, inside the former US Embassy
hotels.whyGo: Eero Saarinen's former American Embassy on Grosvenor Square, reopened in 2025 as an all-suite hotel - the building is a listed piece of mid-century diplomacy and the conversion is the reason to go.
hotels.opNote: Four guides, and a first-hand line on r/FATTravel: "Chancery Rosewood is the best of the list in my opinion and great location too". Rosewood's second London house - not to be confused with Rosewood London in Holborn.

hotels.name: The Connaught
hotels.style: Mayfair institution with a great bar
hotels.whyGo: The Connaught Bar has repeatedly been ranked the best bar in the world, and the Aman Spa in the basement is the quietest room in Mayfair.
hotels.opNote: The bar is open to non-residents and is the reason most people come. Book it - walk-ins at peak are turned away.

hotels.name: The Dorchester
hotels.style: Park Lane, with three Michelin stars in it
hotels.whyGo: Alain Ducasse at The Dorchester is one of the very few three-Michelin-star restaurants in the country, and it is in the building.
hotels.opNote: Five restaurants on site. The Promenade afternoon tea is the accessible one; Ducasse needs booking months ahead and is a separate proposition entirely.

hotels.name: The Emory
hotels.style: All-suite, from the Claridge's owners
hotels.whyGo: Suite-only, from the Maybourne group behind Claridge's and The Connaught, with each floor given to a different designer - Andre Fu, Patricia Urquiola - and Jean-Georges overseeing the restaurant.
hotels.opNote: There are no standard rooms at all; the entry price is a suite. A rooftop Surrenne members' club sits on top.

hotels.name: The Franklin London
hotels.style: Five-star Victorian house on a private garden square
hotels.whyGo: It sits on Egerton Gardens rather than a main road, with the garden square wrapped around it - a residential Knightsbridge address, which is the whole difference between this and the Brompton Road hotels a few minutes north.
hotels.opNote: The widest spread in this batch: two domains in the South Kensington corpus and named again in the dog-friendly, Kensington and general passes. Starhotels Collezione, so the same group as The Gore, also in this batch, and The Pelham. NOTE THE FILING MISMATCH - the corpus that surfaced it is South Kensington but the operator's own page is headed 'Boutique Hotel in Knightsbridge'; the hood follows the operator. No Knightsbridge area guide exists, so areaGuide is empty.

hotels.name: The Goring
hotels.style: The last family-owned five-star in London
hotels.whyGo: Still owned by the Goring family after four generations, with a private garden behind and Buckingham Palace round the corner - the Princess of Wales stayed here the night before her wedding.
hotels.opNote: The only London five-star still in the hands of the family that built it. The garden is residents-only; the dining room is not.

hotels.name: The Guardsman
hotels.style: Small five-star hotel and residences off Buckingham Gate
hotels.whyGo: Six self-contained residences sit alongside the hotel rooms - one, two or three bedrooms each with a private kitchen and dining area, and a private chef and valet available on top - which is a different product from a suite and the reason to pick this over the Broadway hotels round the corner.
hotels.opNote: Two domains in the Westminster corpus and one in the family pass. Two minutes from St James's Park station and six from Buckingham Palace on the operator's own count. BREAKFAST IS A RATE CONDITION, NOT A STANDING INCLUSION: booking direct on the best available rate adds breakfast, a welcome drink and a category upgrade subject to availability, so the breakfast column is deliberately empty.

hotels.name: The Hari
hotels.style: Belgravia independent with a heated terrace
hotels.whyGo: An independent five-star on Chesham Place, between Belgravia and Knightsbridge, with a heated garden terrace that stays usable well past summer.
hotels.opNote: Three of the boutique sources including both Conde Nast editions, and one in the general pass. Independent rather than group-owned, which is unusual at this level in Belgravia.

hotels.name: The Landmark London
hotels.style: Eight-storey glass atrium with palm trees
hotels.whyGo: The eight-storey glass atrium with full-size palm trees in it, opposite Marylebone station - one of the last great railway hotels, and the rooms are among the largest in central London.
hotels.opNote: Four of the family sources and two in the general pass. The room sizes are the reason it keeps appearing on family lists rather than any children's programme.

hotels.name: The Lanesborough
hotels.style: Regency, Hyde Park Corner, butler service
hotels.whyGo: A Regency hospital turned hotel on Hyde Park Corner, with butler service on every floor and a spa in the basement - the most formal of the London grande dames, and it means it.
hotels.opNote: Three domains in the luxury corpus, two in the family one, plus two first-hand accounts on r/FATTravel: "The Lanesborough for sure. Magical!" and a longer one praising the service, the gym and the steam room while admitting "the decor is not my style".

hotels.name: The Langham, London
hotels.style: Europe's first grand hotel, 1865
hotels.whyGo: Opened 1865 as Europe's first grand hotel, opposite BBC Broadcasting House, and the place afternoon tea in Britain was arguably formalised.
hotels.opNote: The Palm Court claims to be the birthplace of afternoon tea and books out well ahead. Conan Doyle and Oscar Wilde both dined here.

hotels.name: The London EDITION
hotels.style: Ian Schrager conversion, 173 oak-lined rooms
hotels.whyGo: Berners Tavern is the reason most people walk in - Jason Atherton's dining room under chandeliers modelled on Grand Central's - and the award-winning Punch Room beside it is the more intimate, speakeasy-style one. The 173 bedrooms above are oak-floored and wood-panelled, closer to a yacht cabin than a hotel room.
hotels.opNote: Two domains in the general corpus and named again in the accessible, Fitzrovia, Soho and boutique passes - five corpora, the broadest reach of this batch. THE HOOD IS FITZROVIA, NOT SOHO: the operator's page title says Soho and its own body copy says Fitzrovia, and 10 Berners Street is north of Oxford Street. It was named by Wheelchair Travel in the accessible corpus, which is worth reading before anyone writes an accessibility claim - nothing here has been checked.

hotels.name: The Londoner
hotels.style: Super-boutique on Leicester Square
hotels.whyGo: Sixteen storeys, six of them below ground, including a private cinema and a subterranean ballroom - built into Leicester Square without dominating it.
hotels.opNote: Michelin calls it a super-boutique: boutique service at large-hotel scale. The rooftop bar looks over the square.

hotels.name: The Mayfair Townhouse
hotels.style: Fifteen Georgian houses knocked together, Wildean theme
hotels.whyGo: Fifteen Georgian townhouses on Half Moon Street run as one hotel, with a dandy-and-Wilde theme carried through the bar - Green Park is at the end of the street.
hotels.opNote: Three guides. Same group as Cliveden and Chewton Glen, so the service standard is the group's rather than a one-off.

hotels.name: The Milestone Hotel
hotels.style: Victorian Gothic, facing the Palace
hotels.whyGo: A Victorian Gothic townhouse directly facing Kensington Palace and the Royal Gardens, with suites converted from the original carriage mews.
hotels.opNote: Each suite is individually themed and priced differently - the Stables suite, built from the original mews, is the one worth asking for by name.

hotels.name: The Ned
hotels.style: A 1924 bank turned hotel and members' club
hotels.whyGo: The former Midland Bank headquarters, built in 1924 by the architect the hotel is named for - marble banking hall, twelve restaurants, and a rooftop pool with St Paul's over the parapet.
hotels.opNote: The rooftop pool is for MEMBERS AND CERTAIN GUESTS ONLY - do not promise it to every booking. The basement spa's 20-metre pool is the one hotel guests can generally use.

hotels.name: The Peninsula London
hotels.style: Purpose-built Belgravia flagship
hotels.whyGo: A purpose-built Peter Marino design at Hyde Park Corner, overlooking Wellington Arch and the gardens of Buckingham Palace.
hotels.opNote: Filed to the Westminster guide because that guide covers Victoria and St James's; Belgravia has no guide of its own and this sits on its Hyde Park Corner edge.

hotels.name: The Ritz London
hotels.style: Louis XVI, Piccadilly, since 1906
hotels.whyGo: The one everybody has heard of, and it still holds up - Louis XVI interiors, a Michelin-starred dining room, and a dress code that is enforced rather than suggested.
hotels.opNote: Four of the family sources. WORTH FLAGGING TO READERS: jacket and tie in most public rooms, and no trainers - it catches people out.

hotels.name: The Savoy
hotels.style: Riverside grande dame
hotels.whyGo: The first luxury hotel in Britain to have electric light and en-suite bathrooms, on the only street in the country where traffic drives on the right.
hotels.opNote: River-view rooms cost substantially more and are the reason to stay. The American Bar is open to non-residents and is the cheaper way in.

hotels.name: The Soho Hotel
hotels.style: Firmdale, hidden behind red brick
hotels.whyGo: Tucked down a mews off Dean Street behind a plain red-brick front, with two private screening rooms and a Botero cat in the lobby.
hotels.opNote: The Sunday film club - a screening plus lunch - is open to non-residents and is the best-value way in.

hotels.name: The Stafford London
hotels.style: Five-star St James's hotel across three separate buildings
hotels.whyGo: Tucked down St James's Place between Green Park and Buckingham Palace, with the American Bar and MICHAEL CAINES at The Stafford - modern European cooking from the Michelin-starred chef - both on site.
hotels.opNote: ASK WHICH BUILDING YOU ARE IN: the hotel runs across three separate buildings with different characters, one of them the 13-room Carriage House across the mews. Named by two luxury guides and, separately, by two afternoon-tea guides - the Lounge and the American Bar are as much of the draw as the bedrooms. Filed to the Westminster guide because that guide covers St James's.

hotels.name: The Twenty Two
hotels.style: Members' club with rooms, Grosvenor Square
hotels.whyGo: A members' club with thirty-one rooms above it on Grosvenor Square - guests get the club, which is the point of staying rather than the rooms themselves.
hotels.opNote: Three guides. WORTH CHECKING before recommending: the restaurant and club are members-first, so a guest's access is not the same as a member's.
